name: Tongan
variant: Standard Tongan with macrons (toloi) and fakauʻa written; everyday (commoners') speech level, with the chiefly and royal levels introduced for recognition
script: Latin with extra letters: long vowels ā, ē, ī, ō, ū (toloi) and the fakauʻa ʻ (glottal stop, written here as U+02BB, not an apostrophe); ng is one letter; 16 letters in all; left to right
basis: Stage 1 follows the Peace Corps Tonga 2009 'Introduction to the Tongan Language' lessons 1–7; the grammar order follows a commercial Basic Tongan course's lecture list (Udemy, Joshua Tanner); topics are checked against the NZ Tongan curriculum guidelines
src: Peace Corps Tonga Training Unit, Introduction to the Tongan Language (lesson packet with audio CD, 2009), files.peacecorps.gov: lessons 1–11 (introduction, alphabet, pronunciation, greetings, useful phrases, numbers, days and months, dialogues); it says it does not teach grammar; no copyright statement found

NZ Ministry of Education Tongan language curriculum material, PDF on nzcurriculum.tki.org.nz (published 2000 by Learning Media; organised as topic units such as Ko ʻAna Koe?; exact title not confirmed in the part read): level 1–3 topics and objectives, the alphabet and fakauʻa notes, and the four speech levels (first 100,000 of about 177,000 characters read). Udemy, Basic Tongan Language (instructor Joshua Tanner): the 16 lecture titles (alphabet and greetings, vocabulary, tense markers, preposed pronouns, postposed pronouns, prepositions, ʻikai, questions, pluralizers, ko e, intransitive and transitive sentences, preposed possessive pronouns); a commercial video course, not a syllabus, and only its lecture list was read

University of Auckland TONGAN 101/101G Tongan Language 1: 2025 course outline (learning outcomes, incl. speech levels and possessive pronouns) and 2019 Canvas syllabus (weekly themes; suggested books Churchward, Shumway, Tuʻinukuafe)
NZ Ministry of Education page for Faufaua! An introduction to Tongan (unit titles only)
Not opened: Shumway's Intensive Course in Tongan and Churchward's Tongan Grammar
note: No university or textbook grammar order was opened. Stage 1 is the Peace Corps packet's order; stages 2–3 follow the Udemy lecture order (tense markers, pronouns before and after the verb, prepositions, ʻikai, questions, plurals, ko e, intransitive then transitive sentences, possessives), which I judged reasonable but which is one teacher's sequence, not an institution's. The family, food, shopping, time, directions and likes lessons and the respect-language lesson come from the NZ guidelines and the Auckland outcomes, placed by my own judgment. The guidelines PDF shows long vowels with grave accents; I wrote macrons as the lead asked. Every Tongan word in the titles was spelled by me or converted from the sources, and should be checked by a speaker. Device voices for to are not checked.
hardest: The fakauʻa and long vowels change meaning (kākā 'cheat', kaka 'climb'), and the stress moves before e / he
Two sets of pronouns: short ones before the verb (ʻoku ou) and full ones after it (au)
Marking who does what: ʻe for the doer and ʻa for the thing in verb sentences
Speech levels: different words for the king, chiefs and everyone else

items: Alphabet and sounds: 16 letters, ng, the fakauʻa ʻ, and long vowels (kākā / kaka)
Stress: on the second-to-last vowel, and the shift before e / he (ʻi he fale)
Greetings and farewells: Mālō e lelei, Fēfē hake? Sai pē, mālō; ʻAlu ā / Nofo ā
Useful phrases: Mālō ʻaupito, Kātaki, Ko e hā e lea faka-Tonga ki he…?
Introducing yourself: Ko hai ho hingoa? Ko hoku hingoa ko…
Numbers 0–100 and money: taha, ua, tolu … hongofulu; paʻanga
Days and dates: Mōnite, Tūsite … Sāpate; Ko e ʻaho hā eni?
Pronouns before the verb: ʻoku ou, ʻoku ke, ʻoku ne
Pronouns after the verb: au, koe, ia; kitautolu and kimautolu
Negation: ʻIkai (no), and ʻoku ʻikai before the verb
Plurals: ngaahi, ʻū, kau (ngaahi fale, kau faiako)
Naming things with ko e: Ko e fale eni, Ko e hā eni?
Questions: ko e hā, ko hai, ʻi fē, ʻe fiha
Verb sentences with no object: ʻOku ʻalu ʻa Sione ki kolo
Verb sentences with an object: ʻOku kai ʻe Sione ʻa e ika
Possessives: hoku / heʻeku (my), ho / hoʻo (your), hono / heʻene (his, her)
Family: tamai, faʻē, tokoua, tuongaʻane, tuofefine
Wants and likes: ʻOku ou saiʻia ʻi he…, ʻOku ou fiemaʻu…
Food and meals: ʻOku ou fiekaia, Haʻu ʻo kai
Shopping and prices: totongi, paʻanga and seniti
Telling the time and the day's routine: taimi, pongipongi, hoʻatā, efiafi
Asking the way: ʻI fē ʻa e…?, ofi, mamaʻo
Speech levels: everyday words and the chiefly and royal ones (haʻu, meʻa)
